lesson.title: The Three-Way Tug of War: Person, Behavior, and Environment
lesson.summary: Reciprocal determinism is Bandura's model showing that personal factors, behavior, and the environment continuously influence one another in a two-way, ongoing loop rather than any single factor simply causing the others.
lesson.body:
Earlier theories of behavior tended to pick one direction of causation and stick with it. Strict behaviorists emphasized the environment shaping behavior. Trait theorists emphasized stable internal qualities driving behavior. Bandura, building on the active, thinking agent described in social-cognitive theory, proposed something less tidy but more realistic: personal factors, behavior, and the environment all influence each other, continuously, in both directions at once.

Picture the three as points of a triangle, each connected to the other two by a two way arrow. Personal factors, including beliefs, expectations, and emotional states, affect how a person behaves. Behavior, in turn, changes the environment a person encounters, and it also feeds back to shape their personal beliefs about themselves. The environment shapes which behaviors are possible or rewarded, and it also shapes what a person comes to believe about themselves and the world. No single arrow tells the whole story, all three keep pushing on each other over time.

Self-efficacy, a person's belief in their own capability to succeed at a given task, is one of the clearest personal factors in this model, and it shows the loop in action. A student with low self-efficacy for math may avoid raising her hand or attempting hard problems, that avoidance is the behavior. The avoidance means she gets less practice and less encouraging feedback from her teacher, which is a change in her environment. That thinner, less encouraging environment then reinforces her original belief that she is simply not good at math, completing the loop and often making the original belief harder to shake, even though it was never entirely accurate to begin with.

The same loop can also run in a positive direction. Modest early success builds self-efficacy, higher self-efficacy encourages a person to attempt harder tasks and persist longer when they struggle, that persistence produces more genuine successes and more positive feedback from the environment, and that feedback further strengthens self-efficacy. Reciprocal determinism is useful precisely because it resists asking whether a person's behavior is caused by who they are or by their circumstances, and instead treats that as the wrong question. In Bandura's model, the person, the behavior, and the environment are constantly remaking each other.
